BHARAT: THE CIVILISATIONAL FOUNDATION OF THE REPUBLIC
Article 1(1) of the Constitution of India
These are not merely two alternative names for a geographical territory. They constitute an important constitutional affirmation of the civilisational identity and continuity of the nation.

India is Bharat. Bharat is not a newly created nation; it is an eternal civilisation rooted in Sanatana Dharma, whose continuity has survived the rise and fall of kingdoms, empires and political orders.

The Indian Republic created by the Constitution in 1950 is not the beginning of Bharat's existence as a nation. The Constitution established the legal and political framework of the modern Republic upon a much older civilisational inheritance.
It is in this context that Sarvjan Sanatan Party (SSP) understands the constitutional expression: India, that is Bharat.
1.2 A Constitutional Republic with a Civilisational Inheritance
SSP's commitment to the Constitution of India as by law established is absolute and unswerving. Every policy will be pursued through constitutional, democratic and lawful means.
Constitutional governance does not require civilisational or cultural amnesia.

SSP considers the Indian Republic the constitutional inheritor and trustee of Bharat's eternal civilisation. The Indian State does not own that civilisation; it has a responsibility to protect, preserve, nurture and transmit it.

The Constitution provides the legal framework of the Republic. Bharat provides the civilisational identity that the Republic must carry forward. These are complementary principles, not contradictory ones.
1.3 The Civilisational Foundation of the Unity of Bharat
The unity and integrity of Bharat extend beyond territorial administration. Long before modern political boundaries, people across the land were connected through shared civilisational traditions.
Rivers, mountains, pilgrimage routes, temples and tirthas.
Epics, Puranas, philosophical schools and systems of knowledge.
Sanskrit, regional languages, festivals and cultural memory.
Traditions and shared values transmitted across generations.
The Unity of Bharat Is Civilisational
These connections created bonds across space and generations. The unity of Bharat is therefore not merely political or territorial; it is fundamentally civilisational.
Public policy must create conditions in which Bharat's civilisational inheritance can continue to develop in freedom, dignity and prosperity for all Indians.
SSP approaches public policy through five inseparable commitments:
Every reform must follow constitutional, democratic and lawful processes.
Preserve, renew, nurture and transmit Bharat's cultural, intellectual, spiritual and civilisational inheritance.
Secure justice, protection, opportunity, livelihood, prosperity and dignity for all Indians.

Each generation is a trustee, not an absolute owner, of its natural, civilisational, social, economic and institutional inheritance. It must preserve and enrich this inheritance for future generations without imposing avoidable debts and liabilities.
Human beings are co-livers with nature and all other living beings. Public policy must protect nature, preserve ecological balance, prevent pollution and promote harmonious coexistence.
For SSP, Civilisational Justice is the harmony of these five commitments. It means ensuring:
Justice and equal protection for all.
Equal opportunity and livelihood for all.
Protection and strengthening of the family.
Revival of Bharat's languages, knowledge traditions and civilisational heritage.
Protection of nature and all living beings.
Fairness between present and future generations.
NATIONAL SECURITY — A FUNCTION OF CIVILISATIONAL ROOTEDNESS
National Security Begins with the People

National security is not created by weapons, armies, police forces or technology alone. These are its instruments. Its deeper foundation lies in the identity, unity and sense of purpose of the people who must defend the nation.
A Nation's Strength Lies in Its Immunity

Just as the human body's health depends on immunity — its ability to recognise and resist disease — a nation's security depends on the resilience of its people against division, subversion and aggression.
A people rooted in their civilisation, conscious of their shared identity and united by a higher purpose are better equipped to withstand internal disruption and external threats.
Internal security cannot be reduced to policing, nor external security to military capability. Both ultimately depend on the strength of the bonds that hold the nation together.
Civilisational Rootedness as a Security Foundation

SSP regards civilisational deracination as a national security threat, not merely a cultural one. When people are severed from their civilisational roots and social identities become instruments of division, national belonging and common purpose are weakened.
Beyond Territory: A Nation Needs a Purpose
A deracinated people may retain the land, but lose the deeper meaning of the nation. Without a higher purpose, people lose what is worth fighting for, sacrificing for and ultimately defending.
Strengthening Those Who Defend the Nation
The armed forces and police must be supported not only by modern capabilities and equipment, but also by a society with a strong sense of belonging, shared identity and commitment to the nation.

Those who serve must understand that they protect more than territory: they protect a living civilisation, its people, values and constitutional order. This understanding gives sacrifice its fullest meaning and national service its deepest purpose.
SSP will treat national security as a responsibility shared by the entire society. This requires two complementary foundations:

This deeper social foundation cannot be created by the security apparatus alone. It must be cultivated through education, public institutions, governance and social policies that shape the values and civic character of every generation.
Hardware enables a nation to fight; civilisational commitment gives it something greater than geography to fight for.
Rebuilding a Secure and United Bharat
SSP seeks to rebuild a Bharat rooted in its civilisation, united by a higher purpose and prepared to defend its civilisation and nation against threats from within and aggression from without.
A Civilisation to Live, Renew and Defend
Bharat's eternal civilisation must not merely be remembered. It must be lived, renewed and defended.
3.1 Bharat Civilisational Heritage and Renewal Mission

What distinguishes Bharat from Pakistan and Bangladesh, which emerged from the Partition of undivided India in 1947, is not geography alone. India, Pakistan and Bangladesh share a common historical and geographical inheritance, but their civilisational trajectories diverged after Partition.
The Indian Republic inherited the eternal civilisation of this land, profoundly informed by Sanatana Dharma, while Pakistan and Bangladesh adopted an Islamic civilisational framework.
Yet since Independence, India's governance model has increasingly undermined the foundation and expression of Bharat's eternal civilisational identity.

For SSP, restoring Bharat's civilisational identity does not mean returning to the past. It means reviving the enduring principles, values and knowledge traditions of Bharat and bringing them into the life of modern India.
Civilisational heritage is not merely monuments, manuscripts, artefacts or their relics. It is a living inheritance expressed through:
Family practices and the relationship between society and nature.
SSP will establish a Bharat Civilisational Heritage and Renewal Mission with two inseparable objectives:
Restore the visible inheritance of Bharat to its original glory.
Renew the living civilisation that gives that inheritance meaning.
Restoration of temples, tirthas, sacred sites, pilgrimage centres and civilisational monuments.
Revival and contemporary application of philosophical, scientific, mathematical, medical, literary, linguistic, artistic and architectural traditions.
Civilisational education and strengthening of Sanskrit, classical and regional languages.
Revival of traditional arts, crafts, music and dance.
Restoration of sacred rivers and water bodies.
Research institutions dedicated to studying, developing and transmitting Bharat's civilisational knowledge.
The purpose is not to turn Bharat's civilisation into a museum. It is to make its civilisational inheritance a living source of knowledge, values, creativity, social cohesion and national renewal.
Bharat Must Embrace Modernity Without Ceasing to Be Bharat.

Civilisational renewal means taking the best of what we have inherited, testing it against the needs of the present, renewing it where necessary, and transmitting it enriched to generations yet unborn.
Modernise without cultural amnesia. Progress without losing identity.

SSP will establish a Bharat Sabhyata Punaruddhara Nigam — Bharat Civilisation Revival Corporation as the dedicated institutional mechanism for the restoration, reconstruction and revival of Bharat's civilisational inheritance.

The Corporation will undertake and support the restoration and reconstruction of temples, tirthas, sacred sites, pilgrimage centres, civilisational monuments and cultural institutions, while reviving the living traditions, knowledge systems, arts and practices associated with them.
Together with annual Government grants as may be required.

A civilisation is not a corpse to be embalmed.
It is a living inheritance to be restored, revived and carried forward.

History cannot be reduced to broken stones, abandoned temples, dilapidated monuments and fading relics. Preserving the remains of a civilisation while allowing its living traditions to disappear is not civilisational preservation; it is the preservation of its decline.
The Bharat Sabhyata Punaruddhara Nigam will therefore restore, reconstruct, revive and bring Bharat's civilisational inheritance back into the living life of the nation.

Other forms of tangible and intangible heritage and living traditions.

FIFTH AND SIXTH SCHEDULES: INTEGRATION WITHOUT ISOLATION
4.4 Fifth and Sixth Schedules of Constitution: Integration Without Isolation
The Fifth and Sixth Schedules have created a constitutional fragmentation of the civilisational space of Bharat.

Large parts of the territories and populations covered by these provisions, historically integrated with India's wider cultural and civilisational geography, were placed under special constitutional regimes that separated them from the ordinary social, economic and institutional life of the nation.

This constitutional segregation has had consequences beyond administration. By isolating populations and restricting their interaction with wider Indian society, it created protected spaces in which external institutional influences, particularly missionary networks operating through education, healthcare and social organisation, could expand with limited competition.

The subsequent religious and demographic transformation of substantial parts of the Northeast and portions of the Scheduled Areas demonstrates, in SSP's view, the consequences of this constitutional isolation.
A constitutional framework that separates territories and populations from the national mainstream weakens social cohesion, economic integration and civilisational continuity.

SSP will repeal the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, together with related constitutional provisions, laws and policies, and replace them with a framework that protects legitimate tribal rights while restoring full social, economic and territorial integration with the rest of Bharat.

The objective is not to erase tribal identity, traditions or legitimate rights. It is to ensure that protection does not become isolation, autonomy does not become separation, and diversity does not become fragmentation.
This is constitutional integration in the service of civilisational unity.

Sanskrit has been the principal language and vehicle of Bharat’s eternal civilisation and its vast corpus of knowledge. Israel’s revival of Hebrew demonstrates how a language that had largely ceased to function as a spoken language can be successfully revived as a living, aspirational language. Bharat must similarly make Sanskrit a living and aspirational language, not merely a subject of academic study.

Sanskrit is one of the world’s highly developed classical languages, with an immense body of literature covering virtually every field of knowledge. Yet there are virtually no Sanskrit-medium schools providing mainstream, high-quality modern education.

Government-funded education up to postgraduate level through enhanced scholarships, irrespective of socio-economic background.

PUBLIC EDUCATION ACCOUNTABILITY AND EDUCATION TO LIVELIHOOD

The quality of public education must be a direct responsibility of those who govern and administer it. A public system cannot be held fully accountable when those responsible for its quality can insulate their own families from its failures by choosing private alternatives.

Those who provide a public service should have a direct stake in the quality of that service. A cook who must eat the food he prepares has a natural incentive to ensure that it is fit to eat. The same principle should apply to public education.

When the children of those who make, fund, administer and regulate public education study in the same public institutions, poor teaching, inadequate infrastructure, weak discipline, unsafe conditions and administrative failure directly affect the families of those responsible for correcting them.

This creates continuous and personal accountability for public education and aligns the interests of those who govern with the millions of families who depend upon government schools, colleges and universities.

SSP therefore proposes that the children of the following study in government schools, colleges and universities serving the locality where the parent is posted or serves, subject to appropriate legal safeguards and necessary exceptions:
Government employees of all ranks and public servants.
Members of Legislative Assemblies and Councils.
Those who govern and administer public education must have a direct stake in its quality.
Public education should be good enough for the children of those who run the State, because it must be good enough for every child of Bharat.

India's education system has become excessively degree-oriented, producing certificates without adequately equipping young people with the skills required for productive work, enterprise or independent livelihood.

SSP will fundamentally restructure education after Class X. Every student must undertake a minimum two-year vocational skill development programme and obtain a recognised qualification in a chosen field. This skill development will be completely free, with all costs borne by Government.
Only after completing the vocational skill phase will a student be eligible to proceed to higher academic education.
Agriculture, animal husbandry and food processing.
Electrical and electronic work, construction and automobile technology.
Other occupations relevant to local economies.
Every young person must acquire at least one economically useful skill before entering higher academic education.
This will promote dignity of labour, entrepreneurship, self-employment, employability and economic self-reliance.

Casteism • De-weaponisation of Caste • Brotherhood and Excellence in Higher Education
7.1 Caste Was Not the Problem; Casteism Is
Caste Was Not the Problem. Casteism Is the Problem.

Varna and jati formed part of Bharat's traditional social organisation, evolving across regions and historical periods. The modern phenomenon of casteism is different: it converts social identities into instruments of discrimination, political mobilisation, institutional division and competing claims of victimhood.

Bharat's civilisational history cannot be understood without recognising the prolonged invasions, political domination, iconoclastic attacks, temple destruction, mass violence, social disruption and economic dislocation suffered by Hindu society under successive foreign regimes for more than a millennium. These conditions contributed to defensive inward-turning, social fragmentation and internal faultlines within Hindu society.

For more than a millennium, Hindu society itself was the principal victim of this violence and political domination. Yet the social condition produced by that prolonged disruption is often presented as though it were the original condition of Hindu civilisation.

If historical Hindu society was a magnificent temple, the Hindu society that emerged from centuries of devastation is, in many respects, a relic of that demolished temple. To condemn the relic without understanding the grandeur of the temple is to invert history.
It shifts attention from those who damaged the civilisation to the condition in which the civilisation was left—and then places the blame upon the victim.

Casteism does precisely this. It takes the internal faultlines of a society severely damaged by centuries of disruption, magnifies them into a permanent narrative of oppressor and victim, and uses that narrative to indict the civilisation that suffered the disruption.

Historical wrongs must neither be erased nor inverted into an indictment of the civilisation that suffered them. Nor should exaggerated, distorted or fabricated atrocity narratives become an industry of permanent victimhood and caste antagonism.
SSP will pursue the elimination of casteism from public life by removing caste as an instrument of political mobilisation and institutional division.
This requires a fundamental review of caste-based reservations, political representation and governance arrangements, with the central question being:
Are these policies eliminating disadvantage, or perpetuating caste as a determinant of opportunity?

SSP's objective is to transcend casteism, heal historical fragmentation and restore civilisational cohesion by progressively replacing caste-based dependence with universal capability and equal opportunity.
The answer to disadvantage is to remove the disadvantage—not perpetuate the identity associated with it.
The State must protect every citizen from violence, discrimination and injustice without creating permanent legal and institutional divisions on the basis of caste or any other identity.

The Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 is a pernicious law that weaponises caste-based legal differentiation as an instrument against other sections of society.
Existing criminal and civil laws already provide equal protection against violence, intimidation, discrimination and other wrongs without weaponising caste.
The law must punish the wrong, not create a different legal standard based on the caste of the parties.
Educational institutions must foster fraternity, shared citizenship and intellectual excellence—not caste consciousness and social antagonism.

Laws and policies that institutionalise caste divisions in higher education will be repealed, including the University Grants Commission (Promotion of Equity in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2026.
Educational Disadvantage Must Be Overcome by Raising Students to the Required Standard, Not Lowering the Standard of Education.

10.1 The Civilisational Purpose of Economic Policy
The purpose of economic policy is not to make the Government rich. It is to make the people prosperous.

Bharat's civilisational tradition does not regard wealth as an end in itself, nor does it regard the creation of wealth as something to be discouraged. Artha is one of the legitimate aims of human life. Prosperity enables families to live with dignity, creates resources for education and healthcare, sustains social institutions and gives individuals the freedom to pursue higher purposes.
The economic role of the State must therefore be to create conditions in which individuals, farmers, artisans, workers, entrepreneurs and enterprises can create and retain productive wealth.
Kautilya expresses the fundamental principle of governance in Arthaśāstra 1.19.34:
“In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare. He shall not consider as good what pleases himself, but what pleases his subjects.”
The prosperity of the State must be derived from the prosperity of society, not the prosperity of society sacrificed for the expansion of the State.
Kautilya also states that the king must remain active because activity is the root of wealth, and that through productive activity abundance of wealth can be achieved.

The same civilisational conception is reflected in Kalidasa's Raghuvamsa, where the righteous ruler's collection of revenue is compared to the Sun drawing water only to return it in vastly greater measure.
Prosperity of Society and the Role of the State

The objective is not an economy in which the State accumulates resources while society becomes dependent upon it. It is an economy in which society itself becomes increasingly productive, prosperous and economically independent.
Government must be strong enough to protect prosperity, but not so extractive that it weakens the productive capacity of the people.
Bharat must seek widespread prosperity, not prosperity concentrated in a few hands.
Moderate Taxation and the One-Sixth Principle
A Civilisational Framework for Moderate, Proportionate and Predictable Taxation
10.2 Moderate Taxation and the One-Sixth Principle

Taxation is necessary to finance justice, security, infrastructure and public services. But taxation that becomes excessive, unpredictable or distortive can weaken production, investment, enterprise and consumption.
Mahabharata and the Principle of Moderate Taxation

The Mahabharata, Śānti Parva, warns against excessive taxation. It compares the kingdom to a cow: if it is milked excessively, the calf becomes weak; similarly, if the kingdom is drained excessively, its people become incapable of achieving great things.
The State Must Not Destroy Its Productive Source
The State must draw resources from society without destroying the productive source from which those resources arise.

Kautilya's discussion of the origin of kingship connects taxation with protection and welfare. In Arthashastra 1.13.6, the historical arrangement assigns one-sixth of grain and one-tenth of merchandise, while also referring to a share in gold. The subsequent passage connects these dues with the king's responsibility for the yogakṣema—the security and welfare—of the people.
The historical system was therefore differentiated, not a universal one-rate tax system.
SSP draws from this broader civilisational principle that taxation must be moderate, proportionate, predictable and justified by the protection and welfare provided by the State.

As a modern adaptation of the civilisational principle of moderate taxation, the maximum aggregate incidence of indirect taxation on goods and services should not exceed one-sixth (about 16%) of their final value.
This proposed ceiling would apply to the combined incidence of applicable indirect taxes, including GST, VAT where applicable, excise duties and other indirect levies.

This is an SSP policy prescription inspired by the civilisational principle of moderate taxation. It is not a claim that the Arthaśāstra prescribed a universal one-sixth tax on all modern goods and services.
The one-sixth ceiling applies to indirect taxation, not to personal or corporate income taxation.

The objective is to prevent taxation from excessively reducing purchasing power, increasing the cost of production and prices, discouraging enterprise or weakening the productive base from which future public revenue itself must arise.
Taxation should sustain the State without weakening the society that sustains the State.
Wealth Creation, Enterprise and Indigenous Technology
Productive Wealth Creation • Enterprise • Technological Self-Reliance
10.3 Wealth Creation, Enterprise and Indigenous Technology

A nation cannot achieve lasting prosperity merely by redistributing existing wealth. It must continuously create new wealth, new enterprises, new technologies, new productive capacity and new livelihoods.

Bharat's civilisational tradition recognises productive activity as essential to prosperity. The Mahabharata identifies agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade and other productive occupations with the prosperity of the people, while Kautilya states that activity is the root of wealth.
“Annam bahu kurvīta” — “Let one produce plenty of food”.
The Taittirīya Upanishad's injunction expresses the civilisational orientation towards abundance rather than scarcity.
The State should therefore not treat wealth creators merely as sources of taxation. They are participants in the creation of national prosperity.

Entrepreneurs, farmers, artisans, scientists, engineers, innovators, traders, manufacturers and skilled workers expand the productive capacity of society. Their success creates employment, investment, technology, enterprise and economic opportunity.
The objective of economic policy should consequently be to make productive activity easier, more rewarding and more widely accessible.
SSP will create an economic environment that encourages productive wealth creation, including through:
Reduction of unnecessary licensing and compliance burdens
Easier access to finance for productive enterprises
Encouragement of manufacturing and productive infrastructure
Support for research, development and innovation
Stronger links between universities, research institutions and industry
Promotion of globally competitive Indian enterprises
Economic self-reliance in the modern world requires technological capability. Dependence upon external sources for critical technologies can create economic and strategic vulnerabilities.
Modern Bharat must therefore not merely consume technologies created elsewhere. It must become a creator, developer and exporter of advanced technology.
SSP will establish a national programme for Indigenous Technology and Innovation, with emphasis on:

Technological self-reliance will not mean technological isolation. Bharat will adopt useful technologies from anywhere in the world while developing the domestic knowledge and productive capacity required to create critical technologies itself.
Bharat must not merely consume the technologies of the future. Bharat must create them.
Wealth creation and technological innovation are not merely private gains; they are means of expanding the productive capacity and prosperity of the nation.
Matsya Nyāya, Fair Competition and Broad-Based Ownership
Fair Competition • Independent Enterprise • Wider Ownership of Productive Assets
10.4 Matsya Nyāya, Fair Competition and Broad-Based Ownership
Economic freedom can be undermined not only by excessive State control but also by excessive concentration of private economic power.

Kautilya's discussion of the origin of kingship begins with mātsya-nyāya—the condition in which the stronger prey upon the weaker. The people seek political authority precisely because they require protection from such disorder.

In a modern economy, the principle has a wider application. Economic domination can arise when enterprises possessing overwhelming market or financial power are able to eliminate viable competitors, control access to markets or progressively absorb independent economic activity.
Mātsya-nyāya must not be allowed to operate in the economic sphere merely because the stronger actor is economically powerful rather than physically powerful.

The objective is not hostility towards large corporations. Large enterprises can create investment, technology, employment and global competitiveness and must be free to grow through legitimate competition.
The concern arises when concentration becomes so great that independent economic life is progressively weakened.

The Mahabharata recognises the importance of traders and other productive groups to the strength and prosperity of the kingdom and instructs the ruler to protect productive activity rather than destroy its foundations.

The modern economic equivalent is clear: a small manufacturer, family enterprise, artisan, trader or MSME must have the opportunity to grow into a larger enterprise rather than being systematically displaced or absorbed because of overwhelming disparities in financial or market power.
Broad-Based Ownership and Fair Competition Framework
SSP will establish a Broad-Based Ownership and Fair Competition Framework to prevent excessive concentration of economic power.
Scrutinise acquisitions that substantially reduce genuine competition
Prevent dominant enterprises from using market power to eliminate viable smaller competitors
Strengthen access of MSMEs to institutional finance
Improve access to technology and markets for smaller enterprises
Prevent discriminatory practices by dominant platforms and enterprises
Protect family businesses, artisans and traditional enterprises
Enable MSMEs to scale into larger Indian enterprises
Encourage decentralised manufacturing and diversified supply chains
Ensure that public policy does not systematically favour excessive concentration of productive ownership
The objective is not to prevent corporations from becoming large. It is to ensure that size does not become a licence to destroy competition, independent enterprise and broad-based ownership.

Economic growth should not be measured only by the aggregate size of the economy. It should also be judged by the extent to which ordinary citizens and families have the opportunity to own productive assets and enterprises.
SSP will therefore promote wider ownership through:
Development of MSMEs and small manufacturers
Support for artisans and traditional producers
Agricultural value addition at the farm and village level
Wider participation in digital and technology-based enterprise
Mechanisms that enable successful small enterprises to scale without being forced into premature acquisition
The objective is not equality of wealth. It is equality of opportunity to create wealth and broad-based ownership of productive assets.
Bharat should create more owners, more entrepreneurs, more producers and more independent livelihoods.
The Economic Philosophy and Ultimate Measure of Prosperity
The economic philosophy of SSP can therefore be stated simply:
People should become prosperous; Government should remain an instrument of their prosperity.
Taxation should sustain the State without weakening the people.
Wealth creation, enterprise, science and technology should expand Bharat's productive capacity.
Economic power must not become so concentrated that the strong can destroy the independent economic life of the weak.
Economic growth must broaden ownership, enterprise and opportunity.

The ultimate measure of economic policy is therefore not merely the size of the Government's treasury, the size of corporations or the rate of GDP growth. It is the prosperity, productive capacity, economic security and economic freedom of Bharat's people.
Bharat must become a nation of prosperous families, productive citizens, independent entrepreneurs and creators of wealth.
The wealth of Bharat must reside principally in the prosperity and productive strength of its people.
India is not a beggar nation that needs foreign charity. There is no free lunch.

Foreign financial contributions can create channels of external influence over India's social, religious, educational, cultural and political life, influencing domestic priorities, public discourse and institutions and, in some circumstances, serving interests contrary to India's sovereignty, social cohesion and national interests.
India's social, educational, religious and charitable institutions must therefore be sustained by Indian society and Indian resources.

SSP believes that regulation is insufficient. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 will be repealed and replaced by a new Foreign Contributions (Prohibition) Act completely prohibiting foreign contributions into India, subject only to narrowly defined exceptions for Overseas Citizens of India (OCIs) acting in their personal capacity.

Contributions by OCIs in their personal capacity may be permitted for the promotion, research and teaching of traditional Indian knowledge and ancient Indian texts, subject to transparency and safeguards and without permitting them to act as conduits for foreign institutional funds.
Non-OCI foreigners and OCIs wishing to contribute for other purposes may contribute to the Prime Minister's Relief Fund or another nationally designated public relief mechanism established by law.
SSP will simultaneously strengthen domestic philanthropy, charitable institutions, religious endowments, community organisations and other Indian sources of social finance.
The objective is not isolation from the world. It is financial sovereignty and national self-reliance.
India's social institutions must be sustained by Indians.
Citizenship for Persecuted Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs
A Constitutional Amendment to Provide Refuge and Citizenship
12. AMEND CONSTITUTION TO GRANT INDIAN CITIZENSHIP TO PERSECUTED HINDUS, BUDDHISTS, JAINS AND SIKHS IN ANY COUNTRY

India is the civilisational homeland of Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh religions. Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs facing religious persecution in any country naturally look to Bharat for refuge, yet many who have reached India continue to live without secure citizenship.
SSP believes that Bharat has a civilisational responsibility to provide refuge and citizenship to persecuted followers of religions that originated in India.

SSP will therefore amend the Constitution by inserting a new Article 11-A to provide for the expeditious grant of Indian citizenship to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs persecuted on account of their religion in any country, subject to identity verification, security screening and other requirements prescribed by law.

The principal basis for eligibility shall be religious persecution on account of being a Hindu, Buddhist, Jain or Sikh. The law shall therefore contain safeguards against fraudulent claims and against misuse of the provision by persons who do not genuinely belong to the protected religious communities.
Bharat cannot remain indifferent when people whose religions originated in this land are persecuted for their faith and seek refuge in their civilisational homeland.
Bharat must provide refuge to the persecuted and citizenship to those who have no other homeland to which they can safely return.
Over-Legislation — A Curse on Modern India
Legislative Restraint • Sunset Clauses • Referendums on Legislation
13. OVER-LEGISLATION — A CURSE ON MODERN INDIA

In Bharat's civilisational tradition, Rajadharma placed the ruler under Dharma; it did not place Dharma under the ruler. The purpose of governance is to uphold justice, protect the people and maintain social order—not to govern society through an ever-expanding body of laws.

Yet modern India has moved increasingly in the opposite direction. Parliament and State Legislatures continuously enact new laws, often overlapping with existing laws, creating increasingly complex regulatory structures and expanding the coercive reach of the State.
Over-legislation has become a curse on modern Indians.

Law-making has too often become a substitute for good governance, effective administration and timely justice. Social problems are repeatedly met with another statute, restriction, offence or regulatory mechanism, even when the real failure lies in administration, enforcement or adjudication.
More laws do not necessarily produce more justice.
Honest administration, competent policing, effective investigation, timely prosecution, impartial adjudication and proper enforcement of existing laws are often more important than another statute.

The State must therefore exercise restraint in the use of legislative power. Legislation should be enacted only when necessary and when its objective cannot reasonably be achieved through better administration, enforcement of existing law or institutional reform.

SSP will amend the Constitution to require that every law enacted by Parliament or a State Legislature contain a mandatory sunset clause and automatically cease to operate after a prescribed period, ordinarily five or ten years, unless expressly re-enacted.
All existing laws will also be reviewed and brought under the sunset framework.

The proposed constitutional amendment will further provide that the people must have the final word on legislation. Subject to specified exceptions, including matters of national security, every law, including constitutional amendments, shall be submitted to the people for approval through a referendum—to the people of India in the case of Union legislation and to the people of the concerned State in the case of State legislation.
Representative democracy must remain an instrument of popular sovereignty, not a substitute for it. Those governed by a law must have a direct constitutional voice in approving it.
The objective is a State that governs less, governs better, legislates with restraint and delivers justice faster.
Vanaprastha — Inject New Blood into Public Life
Generational Renewal • Respect for Experience • Leadership Transition
14. VANAPRASTHA — INJECT NEW BLOOD INTO PUBLIC LIFE

Bharat's civilisational tradition recognised that power and responsibility must pass from one generation to the next. The principle of Vanaprastha Ashrama represented a graceful withdrawal from positions of direct authority, creating space for the younger generation while allowing elders to devote themselves to wisdom, reflection, service and higher pursuits of life.

Vanaprastha was not an abandonment of responsibility. It was a transfer of agency—from control to counsel, from authority to mentorship, and from worldly power towards the pursuit of higher purposes, including spirituality and self-realisation.

Modern public life needs the same principle of generational renewal. When individuals remain indefinitely in positions of authority, opportunities for younger citizens diminish, institutions become stagnant and leadership renewal is delayed. Experience must be respected, but experience should become wisdom and guidance, not a permanent claim to power.

SSP will therefore amend the Constitution to prescribe 70 years as the maximum age for holding positions of authority and leadership in public and private life, including constitutional, statutory, governmental, elected, nominated, political-party, corporate, institutional and other positions carrying significant executive, managerial or controlling authority, subject to appropriate constitutional, legal and ownership safeguards.

The purpose is not to diminish the dignity or contribution of the elderly. After a lifetime of work and responsibility, elders should have the opportunity to withdraw from positions of power and devote themselves to higher pursuits of life—including spirituality, reflection, knowledge, service and the transmission of wisdom to younger generations.
Vanaprastha is not retirement from life. It is the transition from exercising authority to pursuing higher purposes and guiding those who inherit responsibility.
Inject new blood into public life.
Civilisational Impact Assessment of All Laws and Policies
A Civilisational Framework for Law-Making and Policy-Making
15. CIVILISATIONAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT OF ALL LAWS AND POLICIES

A government must look beyond the immediate purpose of a law or policy. Every major decision shapes the society, institutions, economy and culture of Bharat. Governments operate within electoral and administrative horizons; civilisations do not.

The present generation is a trustee, not the absolute owner, of Bharat's natural, economic, social, institutional and civilisational inheritance. It must not consume resources, weaken institutions or diminish the opportunities available to those who come after it.

SSP will therefore establish a Civilisational Impact Assessment (CIA) framework as an integral part of the law-making and policy-making process. The institutional mechanism, authority and detailed modalities will be determined through appropriate constitutional and legislative measures.
A CIA will be required for all laws, policies, programmes and constitutional or institutional reforms. Every such measure will be examined on five fundamental grounds:
Its impact on national unity, security, institutional capacity and self-reliance must be assessed. Policies must be judged in their totality, not merely within departmental or sectoral boundaries.
Bharat's eternal and continuing civilisation must remain capable of transmitting its languages, knowledge, values, traditions, cultural memory and intellectual inheritance.
Modernisation is necessary; civilisational amnesia is not.
Every measure must serve justice, opportunity, dignity, protection and prosperity for all, rather than primarily benefiting a particular constituency, interest group or privileged section.
Does it strengthen the family and social cohesion?
Government should strengthen, not undermine, the family, community and other institutions that sustain social life.
Policies must therefore be examined for unintended consequences such as family breakdown, social atomisation, dependency or permanent sectional division, while respecting legitimate diversity.
Every decision must be assessed for its long-term consequences, including its effects on:
No generation has the right to make those who follow poorer, weaker, less secure or less capable merely for the convenience of the present.
Conclusion — The Bharat SSP Will Rebuild
The Vision and Purpose of the Bharat Rebuilding Plan
16. CONCLUSION — THE BHARAT SSP WILL REBUILD

The purpose of this plan is not merely to propose better government. It is to renew the foundations of national life and enable Bharat to enter the future with confidence in its civilisation, strength in its institutions and prosperity among its people.

SSP will build a Bharat that is just, secure, prosperous, cohesive and self-reliant; where every citizen has access to quality education, healthcare and livelihood; where families and communities remain strong; where enterprise, science and technology flourish; where nature and all living beings are respected; and where economic and political power serve the people rather than dominate them.

SSP will build a Bharat that is modern without becoming rootless; prosperous with opportunity for all; powerful without abandoning justice; diverse without becoming divided; and confident in its civilisation without being closed to the world.
SSP will not seek to recreate the past.
SSP will take the best of what Bharat has inherited, renew it for the present, enrich it through knowledge and innovation, and transmit it strengthened to the generations that follow.

This is the Bharat SSP will rebuild—a Bharat founded on constitutional fidelity, civilisational continuity, Sarvjan Kalyan and justice for every citizen, where the benefits of development, the protection of the State, the opportunities of society and the inheritance of the civilisation are secured for all.
THIS IS CIVILISATIONAL JUSTICE FOR ALL.
THIS IS THE BHARAT SSP WILL REBUILD.
